# Prenatal and postnatal physiology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Basics of pediatrics > Prenatal and postnatal physiology*

[Original Article Link](/library/wo0hVS)

---

## Summary

Fetal and neonatal physiology differ. Prenatally, <u>nutrient</u> and <u>gas exchange</u> occur via the <u>fetoplacental unit</u>. Blood flows from the <u>placenta</u> to the fetus through the <u>umbilical vein</u>, while deoxygenated blood is removed through the <u>umbilical arteries</u> and directed back into the maternal circulation. The <u>fetal circulation</u> has three bypass shunts. Oxygenated blood bypasses both the <u>liver</u> (through the <u>ductus venosus</u>) and the <u>lungs</u> (via the <u>foramen ovale of the fetal heart</u>). The <u>ductus arteriosus</u> allows the deoxygenated blood to bypass the <u>lungs</u> by connecting the aorta and <u>pulmonary trunk</u>. Postnatally, the <u>circulatory system</u> and fetal organs must adapt to the new environment. All three shunts, as well as the <u>umbilical arteries</u> and the <u>umbilical vein</u>, obliterate. The obliterated vessels form <u>ligaments</u>, while the foramen ovale forms the <u>fossa ovalis</u>. Interruption of <u>placental</u> blood supply at <u>birth</u> (i.e., cutting of the <u>umbilical cord</u>) initiates changes in metabolism as well as <u>respiratory adaptation of the neonate</u>. Neonatal temperature regulation occurs via <u>lipolysis</u> of <u>brown adipose tissue</u> and peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u>.

---

## Fetal physiology

The <u>fetal period</u> begins at week 9 of <u>gestation</u> and continues until <u>birth</u>. After the rudimentary structure of the organs is established during the <u>embryonic period</u> (weeks 1–8), the organs begin to grow and differentiate. In many cases, the fine structure and function of individual organs develop slowly. Some organs do not develop completely until after <u>birth</u>. <u>Fetal circulation</u> and <u>fetal organ function</u> differ considerably from that of a child or adult. Intrauterine conditions ensure that <u>nutrient</u> and <u>gas exchange</u> occurs via the <u>fetoplacental unit</u>. The metabolism and <u>hormones</u> are also provided by the mother, especially at the beginning of development.




> [!NOTE]
> Fetal length can be determined on <u>ultrasound</u> starting from week 9 of development by measuring the <u>crown-rump length</u> (<u>CRL</u>). The <u>CRL</u> in centimeters is roughly equal to the square of the month of <u>gestation</u>.

---

## The fetal period

All of the tissues and organs that develop during the <u>embryonic period</u> grow and differentiate during the <u>fetal period</u> (week 9 of development until <u>birth</u>). This period is initially characterized by an increase in fetal size and, from the sixth month onwards, an increase in fetal weight. Fetal body parts do not all grow at the same rate. Head growth, in particular, lags behind the growth of the rest of the body. For more detailed information on <u>embryonic development</u> (first eight weeks after <u>fertilization</u>), see “<u>Embryogenesis</u>”.




| Overview of the <u>fetal period</u> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Weeks of development | Characteristics |
| Weeks 9–12 | <br><br>* Intestinal loops return to the <u>abdominal cavity</u> (week 10).<br><br>* First breathing movements (week 11)<br><br>* The <u>liver</u> is replaced by the <u>spleen</u> as the primary site of <u>hematopoiesis</u> (week 12).<br><br>* Fetal sex can be identified (week 12).<br><br>* Start of <u>urine production</u>, which is excreted into the <u>amniotic fluid</u><br><br>* Fetal waste products are delivered to the maternal circulation via the <u>placenta</u>.<br><br>* Despite a decline in head growth and doubling of the <u>crown-rump length</u> by the end of week 12, the head remains disproportionately large.<br><br>* Limbs have almost reached their final <u>proportions</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Weeks 13–16 | <br><br>* Start of coordinated movement of the arms and legs (week 14)<br><br>* As a result of active <u>ossification</u>, fetal bones are visible on <u>ultrasound</u> (week 16).<br><br>* Rapid growth<br><br>* Head and body <u>proportions</u> adapt to one another.<br><br><br> |
| Weeks 17–20 | <br><br>* Fetal movements become noticeable.<br><br>* The <u>skin</u> is covered with <u>vernix caseosa</u>.<br><br>* Visible <u>hair</u> and eyebrows<br><br>* Body completely covered with lanugo: short, fine, soft, nonpigmented <u>hair</u>, which is replaced by <u>vellus hair</u> during the <u>third trimester</u><br><br><br> |
| Weeks 21–25 | <br><br>* <u>Premature infants</u> can theoretically survive from week 22.<br><br>* <u>Surfactant</u> secretion, which keeps the <u>alveoli</u> open, begins (week 20–22).<br><br>* Ductal development of the <u>alveoli</u> begins.<br><br>* Fingernails start to form.<br><br>* Start of fat deposition<br><br>* Pronounced weight gain<br><br><br> |
| Weeks 26–29 | <br><br>* Many <u>premature infants</u> survive at this stage with intensive medical care.<br><br>* <u>Lung tissue</u> is sufficiently mature to enable <u>gas exchange</u>.<br><br>* The <u>CNS</u> is mature enough to provide central <u>respiratory drive</u> and regulate body temperature.<br><br>* <u>Hematopoiesis</u> begins in the <u>bone marrow</u> (week 28).<br><br>* Eyelids open.<br><br>* Visible toenails<br><br><br> |
| Weeks 30–34 | <br><br>* The fetus responds to light.<br><br>* As a rule, <u>infants</u> survive if born at this stage of <u>pregnancy</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Weeks 35–38 | <br><br>* The fetus is fully mature at 37 weeks of <u>gestation</u> (term <u>infant</u>).<br><br>* Septation of air sacs<br><br><br> |

## Fetal circulation

<u>Fetal circulation</u> must meet the needs of the fetus with the maternal <u>placental</u> supply, as it cannot rely on pulmonary respiration. It must also adapt rapidly to postnatal conditions. While the <u>heart</u> begins contracting in a coordinated manner at the end of week 4, resulting in directed blood flow, development of the <u>fetal circulation</u> extends up to week 9. In <u>fetal circulation</u>, delivery of oxygenated blood and clearance of deoxygenated blood follows the route described below.




### Oxygenated blood




* Direction: <u>placenta</u> (highest <u>O<sub>2</sub>saturation</u>) → <u>umbilical vein</u> (<u>O<sub>2</sub>saturation</u> ∼ 80%; PO<sub>2</sub>30 mm Hg) → <u>liver</u> → <u>inferior vena cava</u> → <u>right atrium</u> → <u>foramen ovale (heart)</u> → <u>left atrium</u> → <u>left ventricle</u> → <u>ascending aorta</u> → vessels of the head, neck, and arm

* First bypass shunt: 50% of the oxygenated blood bypasses the <u>liver</u> and flows from the <u>umbilical vein</u> to the <u>inferior vena cava</u> via <u>ductus venosus</u>.
* Ductus venosus

* A <u>vein</u> that connects the <u>umbilical vein</u> with the <u>inferior vena cava</u>

* Loses its <u>liver</u> bypassing function after <u>birth</u>

* Persists as <u>ligamentum venosum</u> of the <u>liver</u>

* Second bypass shunt: Oxygenated blood bypasses the nonventilated <u>lungs</u> and enters the <u>systemic circulation</u> directly (<u>right atrium</u> → <u>foramen ovale (heart)</u> → <u>left atrium</u>).
* Foramen ovale (heart)

* Opening in the <u>interatrial septum</u> of the <u>heart</u>

* Usually closes during <u>infancy</u> as blood pressure rises in the left side of the <u>heart</u> after <u>birth</u> (see “<u>Closure of the foramen ovale</u>” below)

* A foramen ovale that persists after <u>birth</u> is termed a <u>patent foramen ovale</u> (<u>PFO</u>).





### Deoxygenated blood




* Direction: vessels of the head, neck, and arm → <u>superior vena cava</u> → right atrium→ <u>right ventricle</u> → pulmonary trunk → <u>ductus arteriosus</u> → <u>aortic arch</u> and <u>descending aorta</u> → <u>common iliac artery</u>

* Return of deoxygenated blood to the <u>placenta</u>: <u>internal iliac artery</u> → <u>umbilical artery</u> (lowest <u>O<sub>2</sub>saturation</u>) → <u>placenta</u>

* Supply of the lower limbs: <u>external iliac artery</u> → lower limbs → <u>inferior vena cava</u>

* Third bypass shunt: The ductus arteriosus connects the <u>pulmonary trunk</u> with the aorta and conducts most of the blood directly from the <u>right ventricle</u> to the aorta, bypassing the <u>lungs</u> because of the increased <u>pulmonary artery</u> resistance.





> [!NOTE]
> Ductus arteriosus Directs Deoxygenated blood to the Descending aorta.




> [!NOTE]
> The <u>umbilical vein</u> transports oxygenated blood from the <u>placenta</u> towards the fetal <u>heart</u>, whereas the <u>umbilical arteries</u> direct deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the <u>placenta</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> Because of high resistance in the <u>pulmonary trunk</u>, pressure on the right side of the circulation is on average higher than that on the left side.




### Postnatal adaptation of the circulatory system




| <br><u>Postnatal adaptation of fetal circulation</u> <br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Process | Physiology |  | Postnatal remnant |
| Closure of the ductus arteriosus | <br>* ↑ pO<sub>2</sub> in the <u>pulmonary arteries</u> (due to respiration) and ↓ <u>prostaglandins</u> (due to <u>placental</u> separation), which has a <u>vasodilatory</u> effect → ↓ <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u> and ↑ pulmonary blood flow → reverse flow in the <u>ductus arteriosus</u>  → functional closure of the duct through <u>smooth muscle</u> contraction within a few days → <u>intimal</u> <u>proliferation</u> and obliteration<br><br> |  | <br>* Ligamentum arteriosum: located <u>anterior</u> to the left <u>recurrent laryngeal nerve</u><br><br> |
| Closure of the foramen ovale | <br>* ↑ Pulmonary blood flow → ↑ pressure in the <u>pulmonary veins</u> and <u>left atrium</u> → simultaneous ↓ resistance in the <u>pulmonary arteries</u> → ↓ pressure in the <u>right atrium</u> → functional <u>closure of the foramen ovale</u>  → adhesion of both septa → development of <u>fossa ovalis</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Fossa ovalis</u>: remains as a remnant of the <u>septum primum</u><br><br> |
| Closure of the umbilical arteries | <br><br>* Contraction of the <u>umbilical arteries</u> to prevent blood loss<br><br>* Obliteration within 2–3 months<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Proximal</u> portion of the <u>umbilical artery</u>: remains open and forms the <u>proximal</u> portion of the <u>superior vesical artery</u><br><br>* <u>Distal</u> portion of the <u>umbilical artery</u>: becomes the medial umbilical ligament in the <u>medial umbilical fold</u> of the <u>anterior abdominal wall</u><br><br><br> |
| Closure of the umbilical vein | <br>* Initially remains open after <u>birth</u><br><br> |  | <br>* Later closes to form the <u>round ligament</u> of the <u>liver</u> (included in the <u>falciform ligament</u>)<br><br> |
| Closure of the ductus venosus | <br>* Obliterates after the <u>ductus arteriosus</u><br><br> |  | <br>* Ligamentum venosum: extends from the <u>porta hepatis</u> to the <u>inferior vena cava</u><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> FEEtal patency of the <u>ductus arteriosus</u> is maintained by <u>prostaglandins</u> E<sub>1</sub> and E<sub>2</sub><sub>.</sub>

## Fetal organ function

<u>Fetal circulation</u> and organ function differ considerably from that of a child or adult. <u>Nutrient</u> and <u>gas exchange</u> takes place in the <u>fetoplacental unit</u>. The <u>lungs</u> are not ventilated and are poorly <u>perfused</u>. Other organ functions also develop gradually during the course of prenatal development, some even after <u>birth</u>. The table below provides an overview of the differences between fetal and postnatal organ function. <u>Organ development</u> is not discussed, but can be found in the articles on the individual organs.




| System/Organ | <br>Overview of fetal functional development [[1]](/library/hPYce6) |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Endocrine system</u> | <br><br>* Maternal <u>hormones</u>: <u>Thyroid hormones</u> and <u>glucocorticoids</u> can cross the <u>placental barrier</u>.<br><br>* Fetal <u>hormones</u><br><br>* <u>Insulin</u> and <u>glucagon</u>: formed by the fetus beginning at week 11 of development [[2]](/library/PlXWCy)<br><br>* <u>DHEA</u>: formed in the physiologically enlarged <u>adrenal cortex</u>  of the fetus and used by the <u>placenta</u> for <u>estrogen</u> synthesis<br><br>* <u>Cortisol</u>: formed in the <u>adrenal gland</u> from week 34 of development<br><br><br> |
| <u>Lungs</u> | <br><br>* Fetal breathing movement, despite not being involved in <u>gas exchange</u>, is important for pulmonary development.<br><br>* <u>Distal</u> pulmonary <u>epithelial</u> cells produce <u>chloride</u>-rich fluid that distends the <u>airway</u>.<br><br>* <u>Surfactant</u> <u>lipoproteins</u> produced by <u>type II pneumocytes</u> decrease alveolar surface tension.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Liver</u> | <br><br>* Metabolic function: from week 6 of development<br><br>* <u>Bilirubin</u> excretion: remains the task of the <u>placenta</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> but is slowly overtaken by the <u>liver</u> after <u>birth</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Blood and <u>immune system</u>  <br> | <br><br>* <u>Hematopoiesis</u><br><br>* In the <u>mesenchyme</u> of the <u>yolk sac</u> wall from week 3 of development<br><br>* Later in the <u>liver</u> and <u>spleen</u><br><br>* <u>Gas exchange</u><br><br>* O<sub>2</sub>affinity in <u>fetal hemoglobin</u> (<u>HbF</u>) is especially high to ensure oxygen <u>diffusion</u> from maternal to <u>fetal hemoglobin</u>.<br><br>* This makes the release of oxygen into fetal tissue more difficult.<br><br>* <u>Hemoglobin concentration</u><br><br>* High because of the nature of <u>gas exchange</u> via the <u>placenta</u>, which results in low <u>arterial oxygen saturation</u> (approx. 80%) in the fetus [[3]](/library/1VX2tC)<br><br>* The relative <u>hypoxemia</u> induces hypoxia-inducible factor 1 production, which in return stimulates the fetal <u>kidneys</u> to produce <u>erythropoietin</u>, increasing <u>red blood cell production</u>.<br><br>* <u>Immunoglobulins</u><br><br>* The fetus does not produce <u>immunoglobulins</u>.<br><br>* Maternal <u>IgG</u> crosses the <u>placenta</u> providing <u>passive immunity</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u> | <br><br>* Fully functional in the <u>third trimester</u><br><br>* The fetus swallows <u>amniotic fluid</u> which is absorbed in the intestine and results in the production of <u>meconium</u>.<br><br>* <u>Meconium</u> is usually retained in the bowel until after <u>birth</u> and may sometimes be present in <u>amniotic fluid</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Kidney</u> | <br><br>* <u>Urine production</u> begins between weeks 9 and 12 of development.<br><br>* The ability to concentrate urine develops after <u>birth</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Brain</u> | <br>* Myelination begins in the late <u>fetal period</u> and continues for at least another 10–12 years of life.<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Lung</u> maturity in preterm <u>newborns</u> can be achieved via intramuscular injections of <u>glucocorticoids</u> to the mother which induce pneumocytes maturation and thus the production of <u>surfactant</u>.

## Neonatal physiology

After <u>birth</u>, the shunts of the <u>fetal circulation</u> close to accommodate pulmonary respiration and the cutting of the <u>umbilical cord</u>. After <u>placental</u> circulation is interrupted at <u>birth</u>, the <u>newborn</u> takes its first breath of air. The <u>neonate</u> must now regulate their own circulation (see “<u>Postnatal adaptation of the circulatory system</u>” above), respiration, metabolism, and temperature, which require a series of adaptations. For more information on neonatal care, see “<u>Assessment of the newborn</u>”.




### Respiratory adaptation of the newborn infant




* Initiation: start of pulmonary respiration (after cutting the <u>umbilical cord</u>)

* <u>Lung</u> ventilation: first breaths → <u>alveoli</u> are filled with air;   → <u>lungs</u> inflate → change in pressure conditions





### Metabolism




* Changes: Once the <u>placenta</u> can no longer ensure a continuous supply of <u>glucose</u>, blood sugar levels decrease in the <u>newborn</u>.

* Adaptation: <u>Infants</u> <u>born at term</u> meet their <u>glucose</u> requirements through <u>gluconeogenesis</u> and <u>breastfeeding</u> (or formula).





### <u>Thermoregulation</u>




Normal body temperature of <u>the newborn infant</u>: 97.7–99.5 °F (36.5–37.5 °C)




* Changes: Large body surface area to weight <u>ratio</u> and loss of intrauterine warmth contribute to <u>heat loss</u>.

* Adaptation

* <u>Lipolysis</u> in <u>brown adipose tissue</u> produces heat.

* Peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u> induced by a <u>catecholamine</u> surge reduces peripheral <u>heat loss</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Newborn infants</u> with regulation disorders especially depend on <u>exogenous</u> protection against cooling.
